lead: Triangulation fixes a network of control stations by measuring one side, the base, with great care, and then only angles. Every triangle of the network is solved by the sine rule, so each new side becomes the known side of the next triangle, and coordinates follow from the sides and their bearings. Trilateration does the reverse: electronic distance measurement gives all three sides of each triangle, and the angles are computed. Both build the frame on which detail surveys, road and canal alignments and large-scale mapping are hung.
prereq: You need: horizontal angles by the direction method from Measurement of horizontal and vertical angles, and whole-circle bearings and latitudes and departures from traversing.

blocks.text: A triangulation system is a series of triangles joined side to side. If one side and the three angles of a triangle are known, the other two sides follow from the sine rule: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C, each side opposite its angle. The measured side is the base line; a second base, or a check base, at the far end of the chain tests the whole computation.

The common figures are a chain of single triangles (quick, but with no check beyond the sum of each triangle's angles), braced quadrilaterals (four stations with both diagonals observed, the strongest and most used for a long, narrow strip), and centred polygons (a central station surrounded by a ring of triangles, for wide areas). A triangle is well-conditioned when no angle is below about 30° or above 120°; the ideal shape is an isosceles triangle with base angles of 56°14′, which makes side errors least for a given angle error. Strength of figure is a number computed from the angles of a layout that compares how much angle error grows into side error; a lower value means a stronger figure.

Typical values quoted in Indian textbooks. First-order angles are observed in many sets with a 1″ instrument, so the mean is good to about a second; lower orders accept a few seconds. The sum of the angles of a triangle on the earth exceeds 180° by the spherical excess, about 1″ for every 196 km² of triangle area, so it matters only in primary work.

sections.h3: Field work: stations, signals and the base

items: Reconnaissance. Study maps, walk the ground, choose stations that are intervisible, give well-conditioned triangles, and are easy to reach and to find again. Lines must clear the ground and buildings, keeping well above hot surfaces to limit refraction.

Station marks and signals. Mark each station with a buried mark and a reference sketch. Set up a signal (pole, beacon or lamp) over it for sighting from other stations, and a tower or scaffold where the ground does not give intervisibility.

Angles. Observe directions at every station on both faces and with several initial settings of the circle; reduce each triangle so that its angles sum to 180° (plus the spherical excess), sharing the error equally when the angles have equal weight.

Base measurement. Measure the base by EDM or a standardised steel or invar tape on a cleared alignment. Apply the corrections for standardisation, temperature, pull, sag and slope, and finally reduce the length to mean sea level.

Satellite station. When the instrument cannot stand on a station (a steeple or a tank), observe from a nearby satellite station and reduce the angles to the true station by the small triangles between them.

blocks.text: Reduction to mean sea level:  L₀ = L × R ÷ (R + H) ≈ L − L H ÷ R
blocks.where: L is the measured horizontal length at mean height H above mean sea level, R the earth's radius (about 6370 km), and L₀ the length at mean sea level. H and R in the same unit.

blocks.text: In trilateration every side of every triangle is measured by EDM and reduced to the same surface. The angles are then computed by the cosine rule, cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ (2bc), and used to carry bearings. It is fast where long lines can be measured electronically, and its scale is strong; but a single triangle has no check (any three lengths that obey the triangle rule fit together), so braced quadrilaterals with both diagonals measured are used.

Coordinates are carried through the net like a traverse. From a station A of known easting and northing (E<sub>A</sub>, N<sub>A</sub>) and a side AB of length l and whole-circle bearing β, the departure is l sin β and the latitude is l cos β.
E<sub>B</sub> = E<sub>A</sub> + l sin β;   N<sub>B</sub> = N<sub>A</sub> + l cos β
blocks.where: β is the whole-circle bearing of AB measured clockwise from north. The bearing of the next side is found from the adjusted angle at the station. A station reached by two routes through the net must get the same coordinates from both, within rounding.

examples.question: In a triangulation triangle ABC, AB is a base measured as 500.000 m (horizontal) at a mean height of 250 m above mean sea level. The observed angles, of equal weight, are A = 62°18′10″, B = 57°42′05″ and C = 60°00′00″. A has coordinates E 5000.000 m, N 3000.000 m and the bearing of AB is 75°30′00″; C lies to the left of AB looking from A. (a) Adjust the angles. (b) Reduce the base to mean sea level (R = 6370 km). (c) Find BC and AC. (d) Find the coordinates of B and C, and check C from B.
steps: (a) Sum of angles = 62°18′10″ + 57°42′05″ + 60°00′00″ = 180°00′15″. The triangle is small, so the spherical excess is negligible and the error is +15″: subtract 5″ from each. A = 62°18′05″, B = 57°42′00″, C = 59°59′55″ (sum 180°00′00″).
(b) Correction = L H ÷ R = 500.000 × 250 ÷ 6 370 000 = 0.020 m. Base at mean sea level AB = 500.000 − 0.020 = 499.980 m.
Check from B: bearing BA = 255°30′00″, and turning clockwise through B gives bearing BC = 255°30′00″ + 57°42′00″ = 313°12′00″: sin = −0.72897, cos = 0.68455.
examples.answer: Adjusted angles 62°18′05″, 57°42′00″ and 59°59′55″; base at mean sea level 499.980 m; BC = 511.17 m and AC = 488.00 m; B (5484.06, 3125.18) and C (5111.43, 3475.11) m, checked from B within 0.01 m.

traps: Pairing a side with the wrong angle in the sine rule. BC is opposite A and AC opposite B, so BC = AB sin A ÷ sin C.
Using the unadjusted angles. The triangle's closing error is shared out first, or the two routes to C disagree.
Adding the mean sea level correction. A base measured above mean sea level is longer than its projection, so the correction is subtracted.
Accepting a single-triangle trilateration as checked. Three measured sides always close; only a braced figure or a redundant side shows an error.
Turning the angle the wrong way to get the next bearing. Draw the triangle and check which side of AB the third station lies on.

quiz.q: What is a well-conditioned triangle, and why is it preferred?
quiz.a: A triangle with no angle below about 30° or above 120° (best: base angles near 56°14′). A small error in an angle then makes only a small error in the computed sides, because the sines of the angles are not changing fast.

quiz.q: Why is the base line measured with special care while the other sides are computed?
quiz.a: Every computed side is the base multiplied by ratios of sines, so a fractional error in the base passes unchanged into every side of the network. Angles fix only the shape and are cheaper to observe precisely.

quiz.q: In a trilateration triangle the sides are a = 420.000 m, b = 515.000 m and c = 380.000 m. Find angle A.
Triangle angles of equal weight sum to 179°59′48″. A student adds 12″ to the largest angle only. What is wrong?
quiz.a: With equal weights each angle is equally likely to be in error, so the 12″ is shared equally: +4″ to each. Putting it all on one angle changes the shape of the triangle unfairly and the computed sides by more than the observations justify.

quiz.q: Should a 25 km highway corridor be controlled by a chain of single triangles or by braced quadrilaterals? Justify.
quiz.a: Braced quadrilaterals. A chain of single triangles has only each triangle's angle sum as a check, so an error in one side passes on undetected. A braced quadrilateral has extra diagonals and conditions, giving stronger figures and redundant checks over a long, narrow strip, for a moderate increase in field work.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India carried triangulation chains across the subcontinent in the nineteenth century, and its stations still carry marks today. National control is now built from GNSS baselines and permanent reference stations, adjusted by least squares, and classical triangulation survives in tunnels, dams and deformation monitoring where satellites cannot reach. Search for Great Trigonometrical Survey, braced quadrilateral and strength of figure.
